sources.title: National Museum of Denmark: Saqqaq culture
sources.note: Direct museum research synthesis: chronology, permanently frozen middens and food remains. Saqqaq is an archaeological designation, not a known ancient self-name.

sources.title: Jens Fog Jensen: The Stone Age of Qeqertasuup Tunua, Disko Bugt (2006)
sources.note: Direct author summary of regional research, Meddelelser om Grønland, Man and Society 32. Household reconstructions explicitly inferred from spatial distributions.

sources.title: National Museum of Denmark: Early Dorset
sources.note: Direct research synthesis: resource section and museum-led fieldwork history. Reuses no house claims already attributed to Jensen.

sources.title: Canadian Museum of History: Burin-like-tool, PgHb-1:4017
sources.note: Full indexed original object record verified; direct open returns script shell. Interpretive text places this in Dorset craft context, but formal affiliation field remains to be determined. Broad catalog age 2500 to 700 years ago is not converted to an exact manufacture year.

sources.title: Canadian Museum of History: Drum Rim, PfFm-1:1750
sources.note: Full indexed original metadata: wood, North Baffin, Dorset, outside diameter 173 mm. Performance role is explicitly tentative analogy. Image filenames refer to 1749, so use catalog number 1750 from metadata without claiming image-number identity. Group with burin interpretive work for conservative budget.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art: Old Bering Sea III harpoon counterweight, 2019.456.17
sources.note: Direct metadata and full indexed curatorial description: Alaska, 300 to 500 CE, walrus ivory, 19.1 cm length, counterweight/stabilizer. Animal features are tentative. No exact archaeological findspot claimed.

sources.title: US National Park Service: Birnirk National Historic Landmark
sources.note: Direct site account: small repeated occupations, house construction, low entries, lamps and rare preserved umiak. Its approximate chronology is internally inconsistent in relative-age arithmetic; no precise end date adopted.

sources.title: Claire Alix and Owen K. Mason: Analyzing Early Driftwood Houses of Coastal Alaska
sources.note: Direct research article: geography and driftwood transport, earliest excavated Cape Espenberg houses within a sequence spanning the eleventh to eighteenth centuries. Later metal-cutting examples excluded. Public geometry caveat separately verified against decoded local atlas data.

sources.title: Karen Ryan: Qajartalik 2022, collaborative community-based archaeological fieldwork in Nunavik
sources.note: Direct September 6, 2022 report. Approximately 180 faces; comparative age estimate 1500 to 750 years, not securely direct radiocarbon dates. Eyes/noses/mouths in engraved outlines are a visual witness; no language decoding asserted.

sources.title: T. Max Friesen and Charles D. Arnold (2008): The Timing of the Thule Migration
sources.note: Direct English abstract, American Antiquity 73(3), 527 to 538, DOI 10.1017/S0002731600046850. Site dates support thirteenth-century migration; describe as interpretation, not settled exact first arrival. Spanish abstract mistranslates AD as BC, excluded.

sources.title: T. Max Friesen (2020): Radiocarbon Evidence for Fourteenth-Century Dorset Occupation
sources.note: Direct original abstract, American Antiquity 85(2), 222 to 240, published online 2019, DOI 10.1017/aaq.2019.88. 56 AMS dates from three Iqaluktuuq sites; local continuation past 1300 and temporal overlap do not establish direct interaction.

sources.title: Inuit Circumpolar Council: ICC International
sources.note: Direct institutional self-description: founded 1977, representation across Alaska, Canada, Kalaallit Nunaat and Chukotka, community assemblies. Used for explicitly modern continuity of living communities, not a universal ancient lineage.

batchIdentityNotes.scope: Exact missing HB cultural record, 2000 BCE to 1279 CE. No alias association with Dorset, Thule, Inuit or the existing Newfoundland-focused Paleo-Inuit card. Regional examples explicitly named; source summaries cannot make maps historically precise.
batchIdentityNotes.geometry: Decoded split polygons include Alaska, Canada, Greenland and later eastern Siberia. Dateline plus/minus180 bounds are not global coverage. Qeqertasussuk and Cape Espenberg points outside sampled outlines; Qajartalik inside earlier examples, outside 1200; Birnirk inside.
batchIdentityNotes.chronology: Phases organize a long atlas interval, not succession of governments. Dorset in eastern Arctic and Old Bering Sea in Alaska are contemporaneous regional histories. Migration timing debated; beyond-endpoint 1300 evidence explicitly dated.
batchIdentityNotes.writing: No securely attributable sentence can represent this archaeological umbrella. Qajartalik faces are an authentic visual witness with uncertain age/meaning, not a deciphered script. No modern Inuit phrase substituted for ancient speech.
batchIdentityNotes.evidenceLimits: No ancient school system, clinical treatment or toilet arrangement reconstructed. Household skill and modern collaborative learning supported. Burin formal affiliation uncertain; drum function is analogy. Modern health-care material and later snow goggles excluded.
batchIdentityNotes.region: Americas is the card catalog grouping; this record also includes Siberian polygons.
